content.overview: The plaintiff must prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness. Fraud on the contract and violation of an essential term also bar relief.
content.study: Plead readiness in the plaint. Proof is conduct across the life of the contract, not a sentence at trial. Money-deposit conduct matters in land deals.

learningObjectives: Explain the personal bars to specific performance under Section 16.
Apply readiness and willingness as a continuous factual requirement.
Distinguish incapacity, breach/fraud and substituted performance from the general enforceability rule in Section 10.
enhancement.definition: Section 16 prevents specific performance in favour of a claimant who falls within specified personal bars, including obtaining substituted performance, incapacity or breach of an essential term, fraud or subversion of the contractual relationship, or failure to prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Readiness and willingness under Section 16(c) concerns the claimant's performance of the essential contractual terms according to the true construction of the contract; it must be pleaded and proved through the claimant's conduct.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(a)–(c) and its explanations, read with Sections 10 and 20.
essentialIngredients: Check whether the claimant has obtained substituted performance under Section 20.
Check incapacity, violation of an essential term, fraud, or conduct at variance with the intended contractual relationship.
Require proof that the claimant performed or was always ready and willing to perform essential terms.
For money obligations, apply the statutory rule that actual tender/deposit is not ordinarily required unless directed by the court.
Assess readiness and willingness according to the contract's true construction.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 16 is claimant-specific. It does not ask only whether the contract is legally enforceable; it asks whether this claimant has crossed the statutory personal bar. Readiness concerns capacity and ability to perform, while willingness is demonstrated through conduct. The assessment is continuous and ordinarily extends from the contract through the hearing. The pleading and proof must correspond to the actual obligations under the contract.
examples: A buyer who repeatedly seeks extensions without showing capacity to pay may face a readiness-and-willingness issue. Conversely, a buyer who demonstrates financial capacity and consistent contractual conduct can address the Section 16(c) requirement.
enhancement.distinctions: Section 10 states the general enforceability rule; Section 14 excludes certain contracts; Section 16 bars relief because of the claimant's own circumstances or conduct; Section 20(3) separately prevents specific performance after substituted performance has been taken.

caseLaw.name: J. P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court explained that readiness and willingness must be established from the date of contract to the date of decree, with readiness relating to capacity and willingness reflected in conduct.
caseLaw.relevance: Core authority for the continuous readiness-and-willingness requirement under Section 16(c).

enhancement.problemApplication: In a suit for specific performance, the defendant disputes the claimant's readiness and willingness. Identify each essential obligation, trace the claimant's conduct and financial capacity across the relevant period, and test whether any statutory personal bar applies.
examAnswerStructure: State Section 16 and identify the relevant clause.
List the claimant's essential contractual obligations.
Analyse pleadings and evidence on performance/readiness/willingness.
Address any incapacity, breach, fraud or substituted-performance issue.
Apply the statutory explanation on tender/deposit where relevant.
Conclude whether the personal bar defeats relief.
keyTakeaways: Readiness and willingness is a continuous factual requirement, not a single pleading formula.
The court tests the claimant's actual conduct against the true construction of the contract.
Section 16 must be read with Sections 10 and 20.
